 Robinhood Sinks 12%, SoFi Tumbles 9%, Affirm Drops 8% as Bitcoin Slides and Democratic Congress Weighs on Fintech
 By David Moadel 
 Published November 5, 2026, 2:03pm ET · 3 min read 
 Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel .

 Quick Read
 Robinhood plunges 12% and SoFi slides 9% as Bitcoin's 5% drop and a Democratic Congress ignite a retail fintech selloff.
 Higher-beta lenders get punished while PayPal slips just 2%, showing sellers are targeting volatile growth names over larger payments stalwarts.
 Stifel's Brian Gardner says the Clarity Act is dead for the lame duck, and Elizabeth Warren is poised to chair Banking and probe crypto.

 Retail-facing fintech stocks are taking some of the market’s worst losses as a crypto slide and a political shift in Washington both weigh on the group. Shares of Robinhood Markets ( NASDAQ:HOOD | HOOD Price Prediction ) are at $76.91, down 12% in afternoon trading. That drop puts Robinhood at the front of a selloff aimed at the most growth-oriented names in consumer finance.
 SoFi Technologies ( NASDAQ:SOFI ) stock is at $15.79, down 9%. Meanwhile, Affirm Holdings ( NASDAQ:AFRM ) stock is at $69.60, down 8%. Both lenders are falling much harder than larger payments companies, and that tells you a lot about what sellers are going after.

 Bitcoin’s Slide Puts Robinhood in the Crosshairs
 Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) is trading at $76,003, down 5% over the past 24 hours. This is occurring as investors move out of riskier assets after the post-midterm stock rally of November 4 has faded. Robinhood has the most direct crypto exposure of the three fintechs because digital-asset trading feeds its transaction-based revenue.
 Crypto revenue at Robinhood was already shrinking before this pullback. The company reported cryptocurrency revenue of $100 million in Q2 2026, down 38% year over year (YoY), even as its options, equities and event contracts lines grew. A weaker Bitcoin price tends to cool trading volumes, which keeps that revenue line under strain.
 Washington adds a second worry after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Stifel chief Washington policy strategist Brian Gardner told Yahoo Finance that the crypto industry’s Clarity Act is “off the table for the lame duck session.” Gardner also expects Senator Elizabeth Warren, who’s poised to chair the Senate Banking Committee, to pursue investigations targeting crypto firms along with Wall Street banks and private equity firms. That outlook raises the regulatory stakes for Robinhood and its crypto-linked fintech peers.
 Robinhood, SoFi and Affirm Fall Harder Than PayPal and Block Inc.
 Larger payments names are sliding far less. PayPal Holdings ( NASDAQ:PYPL ) stock is at $58.82, down 2%. Moreover, Block ( NYSE:XYZ ) stock is at $84.24, down 4%. The gap suggests sellers are hitting the higher-growth, more volatile fintech names hardest, and Robinhood, SoFi and Affirm all fit that profile.
 Affirm’s next earnings report is still ahead, which gives the company a chance to shift the conversation after the selloff. On August 27, chief executive Max Levchin stated the fiscal fourth quarter was “our most profitable quarter ever, even without the tax allowance release.” Levchin also told analysts, “Our consumer is doing fine.”
 How Robinhood, SoFi and Affirm Make Their Money
 Robinhood earns most of its revenue from trading in options, equities, event contracts and crypto, plus interest on margin loans and customer cash, and that transaction-heavy mix ties Robinhood’s results to retail trading appetite, which tends to fade when Bitcoin and speculative stocks fall together. The company’s reliance on payment for order flow (PFOF) also leaves it exposed to tougher rules from Washington.
 SoFi runs as a digital bank with its own charter and funds personal, student and home loans with member deposits. This structure makes SoFi more sensitive to credit conditions and interest rates than to crypto prices, though the company does offer crypto trading through SoFi Crypto.
 Affirm operates a buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) network. The network earns merchant fees and consumer interest, and Affirm funds its loans through warehouse lines, securitizations and loan sales. Growth at Affirm depends on adding merchants and keeping credit steady, and BNPL lending has drawn scrutiny from regulators and lawmakers.
 Fintech Selloff Faces Jobs Data and a New Congress
 The broad market is giving back the post-midterm rally of November 4, with technology stocks leading the decline. October’s jobs report comes out on November 6, and it’s the next macro test for rate-sensitive lenders like SoFi and Affirm.
 Robinhood’s next test is whether Bitcoin stabilizes enough to bring crypto trading back to its platform. Optimists can point to Robinhood’s growth in options, equities and prediction markets, which has helped offset its weaker crypto revenue. If Warren takes the Senate Banking Committee chair, crypto legislation could slow while scrutiny of the industry broadens.
 SoFi and Affirm face a different question, one centered on credit health and funding costs as much as crypto. Traders may prefer to keep their exposure smaller until the regulatory and crypto uncertainty resolves.
